summary:
1. What have we developed?
Earth Trends (Data Detective) is a web app for investigating climate change anywhere on Earth. Users search or click a place on a NASA-layer map, choose a variable (temperature, rainfall, clouds, humidity, sunlight or wind), and the app fetches real NASA POWER data. It then removes seasonal cycles, fits a trend, runs a robust Mann-Kendall test, and gives a plain-English verdict with the p-value. It is built with React, Fast API and SQLite.

2. How does it address the challenge?
It lets anyone be an Earth system trend detective. A guided wizard walks users through finding a variable, detecting a trend and judging whether it is significant. It also explains why a trend may happen (urban heat, deforestation, drought), compares two places, and shows how many more years of data are needed to be sure.

3. Why is it important?
NASA data is open but hard to interpret. Our app turns it into trustworthy, understandable evidence for students, citizens, journalists and planners. It is honest about limits: a trend shows change, not its cause.🚀
details:
NASA Data

Our project uses NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), which provides satellite and model-based data from MERRA-2 and CERES for any latitude and longitude. We use six variables: air temperature (T2M), rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), cloud cover (CLOUD_AMT), relative humidity (RH2M), sunlight (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN) and wind speed (WS2M). We fetch monthly and daily time series from 1984 to the last full year and use them to detect long-term trends. We also show NASA GIBS satellite layers on the map: satellite photo, cloud fraction, land-surface temperature and IMERG rain rate. NASA data is the core of the project: every trend, p-value and verdict comes from real NASA data.

I also wrote a fuller Project Details answer, in case it needs more detail:

What does it do / how does it work?

Earth Trends (Data Detective) is a web app that helps anyone find out whether the climate of a place is really changing. The user searches for a place or clicks it on a full-screen Earth map and chooses a variable: temperature, rainfall, clouds, humidity, sunlight or wind. Our Python backend fetches real NASA POWER data and stores it in a database so repeat requests are instant. The app removes the seasonal cycle, fits a trend line, and reports the change per decade with a p-value. It also runs a robust Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope as a second check. The result becomes a plain-English verdict: significant trend, not yet significant, or inconclusive. A slider shows how many more years of data are needed to be sure.

Benefits

It makes NASA climate data easy for people with no statistics background. It gives a clear answer in seconds for any place on Earth, explains why a change may happen (for example urban heat or deforestation), and is honest about its limits.

Intended impact

To improve climate and data literacy for students and citizens, and to give journalists, teachers and local planners quick, evidence-based answers about local change.

Tools and technology

JavaScript (React, Vite, Chart.js, MapLibre GL), Python (FastAPI), SQLite, NASA POWER and NASA GIBS data, and OpenStreetMap. No special hardware was needed. It runs on a normal laptop and browser.

How is it creative?

It works like a detective story: ask a question, test the evidence, then deliver a verdict. It has a “how many more years of data do we need?” slider and uses two statistical methods to cross-check results. It also puts real NASA satellite layers on an Earth-themed map.

Factors considered

Scientific honesty (seasonal noise, and a trend is not a cause), ease of use for non-experts, reliability (caching and fallbacks if NASA is down), and the 50 km resolution of the data.
